examples.text: All forms of matter—solid, liquid, and gas—have mass and take up space!
Matter is anything that has mass and takes up space, just like a rock, water, and even air!

How many forms does matter come in?

Three: solid, liquid, and gas!
All forms of matter—solid, liquid, and gas—have mass and take up space!
A solid keeps its own shape and volume, even when you move it to a completely different container!
Solid modeling clay can be molded into new shapes! It remains a solid because its definite volume does not change.

How does a liquid behave in a new cup?

A liquid has a fixed volume, but it takes the shape of whatever container holds it!

Does a liquid keep the same volume when it changes shape?

Yes! A liquid changes shape but keeps the same amount of space (volume).
Even though gas particles like oxygen expand to fill their container, they still take up space and possess volume!

What shape does a gas have?

A gas has no fixed shape — it spreads to fill its whole container, like air in a balloon!
Ice is simply water in its solid form — water that has frozen and turned hard because of the cold! ❄️

Is your brain mostly solid or liquid?

It's a soft solid organ, but composed of nearly 80 percent liquid water!
A graduated cylinder is a marked container used to measure the volume of a liquid!

What is a beaker used for in the lab?

It’s a glass container with side markings! Scientists use it to measure the exact volume of a liquid.
The volume of a liquid is usually measured in liters (L) and milliliters (mL)!
Did you know that one whole liter is exactly equal to 1,000 milliliters? That is a lot!
Look at water in a narrow glass — it curves up at the edges! This U-shape curve is called a meniscus, caused by water adhering to the glass.
The meniscus is the curve liquid makes in a container. Water has a concave meniscus! Always read the bottom of the curve at eye level for an accurate measurement.
Ice melts (turns to water) at 0 degrees Celsius (0°C)!
Cold ice cream melts and turns into a liquid when left in a warm place!
When water freezes, it magically turns into solid ice!
When a liquid is cooled enough, it freezes and turns into a solid!
We boil sweet cane juice until the water evaporates, leaving yummy sugar crystals behind!
Heat from the Sun causes liquid water in Laguna de Bay to evaporate into invisible water vapor!
Thick morning fog forms when water vapor cools down and condenses right close to the ground!
Those tiny dew drops on grass? They form by condensation, when water vapor turns into liquid!

A simple investigation has four steps: state the question or problem; list the materials you need; describe and follow your procedure; report what you found out from your observations. Your findings should answer the original question.
A simple science plan fits on one page! Just include the problem, the materials, the steps to do, and what you found out.
We usually measure mass in grams (g) and kilograms (kg)!
Here is a fun fact: One single gram is equal to a whopping 1,000 milligrams!
Ice melts (turns to water) at 0 degrees Celsius (0°C)!
Water freezes and turns into ice at exactly 0 degrees Celsius (0°C)!
Taring means setting the balance to zero with the empty container on it, so only the liquid gets weighed.
Blow up a balloon and put it on a balance — the air inside actually adds real, measurable mass!

How do we measure the mass of an object?

We use a special balance to measure the mass of an object!
Taring means setting the balance to zero with the empty container on it, so only the liquid gets weighed.
Most of the saliva in your mouth is actually water — it helps you chew and swallow your food.
The mouth is food's first stop in digestion: teeth crush it as mechanical breakdown, while saliva starts breaking it down chemically.

What is the esophagus for?

The esophagus is the muscular tube that carries the food you swallow all the way from your mouth down to your stomach.
Your stomach has strong juices, or acid, that help break down all the food you eat.
Your stomach makes strong hydrochloric acid to break down food and kill any bacteria you swallow.
Tiny villi inside your small intestine increase its surface area, helping nutrients from digested food pass efficiently into your bloodstream.

How long is your small intestine?

Your small intestine is about twenty feet long, and it's where your body absorbs most of the nutrients from your food.
Fiber from veggies and fruit isn't digested, but it helps your large intestine push waste along and keeps constipation away.
In the large intestine, the body absorbs water from leftover food, making the waste more solid.
Your nose cleans and warms the air before it reaches your lungs.
Every time you breathe in, air rushes into your body through your nose and mouth!
Your windpipe splits into two tubes, one leading into each lung.
Follow the air! It goes in through your nose, down your windpipe, then straight into your lungs.
Inside the lungs are millions of tiny air sacs called alveoli, where oxygen passes into the blood.
In our lungs, oxygen passes into the blood by diffusion from the air, where it's more concentrated!
After an ovary releases an egg cell, it travels toward the uterus through a connecting tube!

Where are egg cells made?

Egg cells are made in the ovaries! They are not made in the uterus, and not in the vagina either.

What does the uterus do?

The uterus is a hollow, muscular organ in your lower belly that holds and protects a growing baby!
The thick muscle walls of the uterus can stretch slowly to make room for a growing baby inside!
To spot the vagina on a picture, just find the tube that links the uterus to the outside of the body!
In a labeled picture, the vagina is the passageway drawn right below the uterus, opening to the outside!
The prostate makes fluid that forms part of semen. This fluid helps support sperm. The testes make sperm; the prostate adds fluid.
A boy has two testes! These oval organs make sperm, which are the male sex cells.
Front-view diagrams show your left and right testes or ovaries as a pair. Side-view diagrams show the depth from front to back!
Inside the penis runs a special tube that can carry either urine or the fluid containing sperm!
The penis works with the testes and prostate by providing the pathway that lets sperm leave the body!
A classification table has rows and columns! You can line up living things and see which characteristics they share.
Reptiles such as lizards and snakes have dry skin covered with scales and breathe air with lungs. These shared features help us group them in a classification table.
Santol, atis, and guyabano all grow flowers first, and those flowers later turn into the fruit we eat.
Calamansi and dalandan grow on small trees—the trees bloom with flowers first, then those flowers turn into fruit.
Mosses are tiny flowerless plants that grow packed together, forming a soft green carpet!
A fern (pako) is a leafy green plant with broad or finely divided leaves, but it never grows flowers.
A goat is a mammal that makes milk to feed its babies.
The monkey is a mammal, so it has fur and feeds its baby with milk.
Reptiles like snakes and lizards have dry, scaly skin.
A sea snake is a reptile that spends almost its entire life living in the ocean.
Arachnids like spiders have no antennae, but insects do.
An insect's body has three parts: the head, the thorax, and the abdomen.
The fruit dove, also called punay, is a kind of pigeon with very colorful feathers.
Birds are the only animals that have feathers, which keep them warm and help them fly.
Humans breathe air with lungs, but fish pull oxygen straight from the water using their gills.

Why is it called a lionfish?

Because it has big fan-like fins that spread out like a lion's mane!
Frogs and salamanders are 'cold-blooded' too — their body temperature follows the warmth or coolness of the water and air around them.
Besides its lungs, a frog can breathe through its wet skin — oxygen passes right through into its blood, so it can stay underwater a long time!

What is that fuzzy stuff on old bread?

It's mold — a fuzzy fungus that grows on old food like bread.

Is a mushroom a plant?

No! A mushroom is a fungus, not a plant — it has no leaves or roots and can't make its own food from sunlight.
Bacteria come in different shapes — round like a ball, long like a stick, or curly like a spring!
The most important steps of the nitrogen cycle are carried out by tiny bacteria — making them essential partners for all of nature.
The tamaraw is a mammal that feeds its young with milk.
Most mammals give birth to live babies and feed them with milk.
Like other birds, penguins lay eggs to have their young.
The hummingbird lays the smallest egg of any bird in the world!
A baby carabao drinks its mother's milk first, and only learns to eat grass when it grows older!
Unlike mammals, birds do not nurse their babies with milk; they bring insects, seeds, or worms to feed their chicks!
Baby chicks have soft down feathers that keep them warm until stronger flight feathers grow in.
The hard eggshell isn't just a shell — it's a tiny armor that keeps the baby chick safe inside.
When the soil is wet and warm, a rice seed sprouts and grows into a small seedling.
Before its first leaves appear, a seedling uses the food stored inside the seed as its starting energy.
Unlike mammals, birds do not nurse their babies with milk; they bring insects, seeds, or worms to feed their chicks!
Every life cycle repeats when a grown animal or plant makes offspring, and those offspring grow up to make their own!
Seagrass spreads underwater through creeping stems called rhizomes that grow beneath the sand.
The ginger plant's leaves make food using sunlight, and the rhizome stores that food safely underground.
Sweet potato stores starch in its swollen roots, which we eat — and cassava also has tuberous roots, not a tuberous stem.
A potato is actually an underground stem called a tuber, and its 'eyes' are buds that can sprout into new plants.
The makahiya plant has small thorns on its stem that give it extra protection from animals.
Some vines use tiny hooks or thorns to snag onto a nearby plant as they climb upward!
A bulb, like garlic or onion, is an underground part of a plant that stores food to keep it growing.
Onions and garlic grow from bulbs — a plant part that stores food and can sprout into a brand-new plant!
Orchids grow special aerial roots that reach into the air, soaking up water and nutrients from rain and humidity — not just from soil!

Why do some orchids have roots in the air?

Many orchids growing on trees have aerial roots out in the open air, which they use to cling to branches and soak up water from rain and dew.
The kapok tree drops all its leaves during the dry season, before it flowers.
Storing water inside its body is a plant's clever trick for surviving in hot, dry places.
Mangroves along Philippine coasts have special roots that can survive in salty seawater.
A pitcher plant has a lid on top that keeps rain from flooding in and watering down the liquid inside.
Some predators like tigers also use camouflage and creep quietly, so they can suddenly attack their prey.
Camouflage isn't just for hiding from danger — predators like lions use it too, sneaking close to their prey before they attack!

What is Batesian mimicry?

It's when a harmless animal copies the look of a dangerous one, so predators leave it alone.

Which sea creature can copy other animals?

The mimic octopus changes its color and shape to imitate other sea animals, like sea snakes!

Which way will an object move when pushed or pulled?

Every force has a direction! An object moves in the direction of the push or pull.

Where exactly does an object go when a force acts on it? Let's explore the science!

Every force has a direction! An object moves toward where it is pushed or pulled.

What happens in a simple ball investigation on a flat table?

When you gently push it with your finger, the ball rolls exactly in the direction your finger pushes across the flat table!
Fish have slippery, slimy skin that lowers friction with the water! This helps them swim quickly and smoothly.
Keep the ramp height the same for every test! A higher ramp gives the car more speed, hiding the surface's true effect.
Keep the ramp height the same for every test! A higher ramp gives the car more speed, hiding the surface's true effect.
The written method is so clear that another person could follow the same steps and check if the results come out the same!
Because of friction, part of the work we do is wasted as heat!

Why do your palms get warm when you rub them together?

The friction makes heat!
An object with wheels is much easier to push because the wheels reduce friction!
The wheels of a kariton reduce friction—the rubbing against the ground—so a heavy load moves easily!
Friction helps us not slip, just like the good grip of shoes on the floor!

How do fishermen hold a wet, slippery net?

The knots and threads create friction, letting them grip it tightly!
Most forces need to touch an object, but gravity, magnetism, and static electricity can push or pull without touching at all!

Do all forces need to touch something to work?

Most forces need touch, but magnets and gravity can act without touching! A magnet pulls metal from a distance.
If you drop a feather and a hammer in the Moon's vacuum, they hit the ground at the exact same time!
In a vacuum with no air resistance, heavy and light objects fall at the exact same rate, just like Galileo showed!
As an object falls, it keeps speeding up because gravity never stops pulling on it!
A falling coconut gains kinetic energy as gravity pulls it faster toward the ground!
Rub a balloon on your hair and it gains static electricity that makes it stick to a wall like magic!
Combing dry hair with a plastic comb builds up static electricity that easily attracts small paper bits!
Clothes that rub against each other build up static, which makes them cling together!
Rub a balloon on your hair and it gains static electricity that makes it stick to a wall like magic!
A battery stores chemical energy and turns it into electrical energy when connected in a circuit!
For electricity to flow, it needs a complete closed path called a circuit, going out from the battery and back!
When a switch is turned off, it breaks the path so electricity can no longer flow through the wire!
A switch is a handy electrical component! You use it to open or close a circuit and control current flow.
For electricity to flow, it needs a complete closed path called a circuit, going out from the battery and back!
A switch opens and closes the flow of electricity! When the circuit is closed, current flows and the light turns on.
Scientists draw circuits using special symbols! A line means wire, a short-and-long line pair means battery, and a circle with a cross means bulb. That's a circuit diagram!

How do we draw a battery in a circuit diagram?

A cell is drawn as a long line (positive!) and a short line (negative!). Several cells in series? That's alternating long-short-long-short lines!
Graphite, the material inside your pencil, is a cool nonmetal that can still conduct electricity!
A conductor is a material that lets electricity flow through it easily—like copper and other metals!
Glass is an electrical insulator, so it is used on power line poles to keep electricity from leaking out!
Electrical wires have a rubber coating because rubber is an insulator that prevents dangerous electric shocks.
In a circuit test, materials like paper, wood, and plastic will not make the bulb light up because they are insulators.
Place an object in a circuit, and if the light turns on, it is a conductor! This means it lets electricity flow, just like metal.
Placing a piece of iron inside the wire coil makes the electromagnet much, much stronger!
You can build a simple electromagnet by wrapping wire around a nail and connecting the ends to a battery!
Placing a piece of iron inside the wire coil makes the electromagnet much, much stronger!
When electric current flows through a wire, it magically creates a magnetic field all around the wire!
A marsh is a treeless wetland filled with grasses, reeds, and other low plants!
Ocean currents carry plankton, fish eggs and larvae, and other tiny animals to distant parts of the sea!
A mountain is a super tall landform with steep sides! It is much higher and bigger than a hill.
The Cordillera in northern Luzon is a large mountain range and home of the famous rice terraces!
Weathering and erosion are usually very slow! It can take thousands of years to fully change the shape of a mountain or valley.

How do rivers shape the land?

As water flows downhill in rivers, it slowly carves and reshapes the land, forming valleys over time!
When a river overflows, it leaves rich mud on both banks, building a fertile flat land called a floodplain!
Some marshes are freshwater marshes near rivers and lakes, while others are saltwater marshes near the coast!
Some marshes are freshwater marshes near rivers and lakes, while others are saltwater marshes near the coast!
The tangled roots of mangroves trap mud carried by water, slowly building up and stabilizing the coastal land!
Garnet is a beautiful mineral that is most commonly known for its deep red color!
The birthstone for December is the turquoise, a beautiful gem with a lovely blue-green color!
Comparing granite from two different provinces shows that the same rock type can vary in color and grain size from place to place!

Why can't we always trust a mineral's color?

Color alone isn't always reliable for identifying a mineral because one mineral can come in many different colors!
Every question in a dichotomous key asks about something you can see or test on the rock — never its name!

What makes a good rock classification record?

A great record lists the rock's properties, the exact answers you chose in the key, and the final rock name!

What makes a good rock classification record?

A great record lists the rock's properties, the exact answers you chose in the key, and the final rock name!
Before starting the key, write each rock's features in a table so you never forget what you saw!
Soil is a cool mix of fine rock bits and decayed plants and animals!
Waves pounding the shore slowly break large rocks into smaller and smaller pieces!
Volcanic ash from Mayon Volcano adds lots of minerals to the local soil, helping abaca plants grow strong and healthy!

Is soil just crushed rock?

Nope! Soil is a cool mix of weathered minerals, decaying organic matter, water, and trapped air!
A glacier is a huge mass of ice that slowly moves and carves out wide valleys as it drags rock!
Erosion is the carrying away of broken rock and soil by water, wind, or ice to a completely new place!

With your teacher, put soil in a shallow tray and tilt it slightly over a basin. Slowly pour a little water at the higher end. Watch soil move with the water: this models erosion. Keep the tray away from electrical equipment and wash your hands afterward.

How does the water cycle work?

In the water cycle, water evaporates from the sea, condenses into clouds, and falls back down as rain!

How are clouds made?

Warm ocean water evaporates into invisible water vapor, which later condenses to form the visible clouds we see in the sky!
Rain forms high up in the sky when water vapor in the clouds condenses into tiny water drops!
Rain from the water cycle refills dams like Angat! This supplies fresh drinking water to Manila.

How does a simple bag show the water cycle?

In a water-cycle-in-a-bag experiment, the Sun's heat evaporates the water, and the vapor condenses on the cool sides to trickle down like real rain!
A water cycle model placed in sunlight shows more evaporation and condensation than one kept in the shade.
A flood is simply water that covers land which is usually dry!
Heavy rain that lasts a long time is the most common cause of floods!
Signal No. 4 means expected winds of 118 to 184 km/h.
Signal No. 5 means winds of 185 km/h or higher, the level of a super typhoon!
After the cyclone, it's messy outside! You'll see fallen branches, mud, and downed lines, even if the wind is lighter.
Even when the sky looks calmer, floodwater may still stand in streets and fields! The after-weather includes leftover water, not just sunshine.
Early before-the-storm hours can trick you! One town might look fine, while the cyclone is already wet and windy nearby.
Before land winds peak, the sea along the path grows rougher! Bigger swells appear, making the weather unsafe for small boats.

Why do streets and rivers flood during a storm?

The rain is heavy and lasting! Streets and rivers can flood, even while the strong wind is the main danger.

What is the weather like during a cyclone?

It brings very strong, gusty wind! This can break branches, peel roofs, and make walking outdoors totally unsafe.

Where is the Sun in our solar system?

The Sun is at the center of the solar system, with the planets orbiting around it!

What keeps Earth and other planets from flying off into space?

The sun! It sits at the center of our solar system. Its pull, called gravity, keeps planets on their paths. It takes Earth one year to orbit!
An asteroid is made of rock and metal, while a comet is made of ice, dust, and rock!
Ceres is the largest object in the asteroid belt and is also considered a dwarf planet!
The four inner planets are rocky! These are Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars.
Jupiter is the largest planet, while Mercury is the smallest. But Earth is the biggest of the rocky planets!
During a full moon, the Earth is between the Sun and the Moon, letting us see its entire bright, lit face!

Why can't we see the Moon during a new moon?

During a new moon, the Moon is between the Earth and the Sun, hiding its lit side from us!
You can show Moon phases with a ball and a lamp! As the ball circles you, you see different amounts of its lit half — just like the real Moon lit by the Sun.
To draw moon phases, place the Sun on one side and Earth in the middle. Then, show the Moon in different positions around Earth!
